sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In this analysis, we aimed to systematically compare the clinical outcomes observed with rivaroxaban versus low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) [enoxaparin] for thrombo-prophylaxis following total knee arthroplasty (TKA).

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Relevant studies based on rivaroxaban versus LMWH for thrombo-prophylaxis following TKA were searched through online databases. Data sources were MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane database, Google scholar, www.ClinicalTrials.gov and Web of Science. Nine studies with a total number of 26,675 participants were included. Clinical outcomes (adverse efficacy and bleeding outcomes) were considered as the endpoints in this analysis. The Revman software was used for data analysis. Risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were used to represent the results.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A total number of 26,675 participants were included in this analysis whereby 13,496 participants were assigned to rivaroxaban and 13,179 participants were assigned to LMWH. Our current results showed that deep venous thrombosis (RR: 0.60, 95% CI: 0.51 – 0.71; P = 0.00001), venous thromboembolism (RR: 0.56, 95% CI: 0.45 – 0.70; P = 0.00001), and all-cause mortality (RR: 0.54, 95% CI: 0.33 – 0.87; P = 0.01) were significantly lower with rivaroxaban compared to LMWH for thrombo-prophylaxis after TKA. Adverse cardiac events (RR: 1.50, 95% CI: 0.53 – 4.21; P = 0.44) were similarly manifested. However, any bleeding event (RR: 1.18, 95% CI: 1.07 – 1.31; P = 0.001), major bleeding (RR: 1.54, 95% CI: 1.12 – 2.11; P = 0.008), non-major bleeding (RR: 1.15, 95% CI: 1.01 – 1.30; P = 0.03), minor bleeding (RR: 1.19, 95% CI: 1.06 – 1.32; P = 0.002) and bleeding leading to re-operation (RR: 1.62, 95% CI: 1.08 – 2.44; P = 0.02) were significantly higher with rivaroxaban when compared to LMWH.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Our analysis showed that rivaroxaban when used as thrombo-prophylaxis following TKA, significantly reduced thrombotic outcomes when compared to LMWH. However, the risks of bleeding events including major and minor bleeding events were significantly increased in comparison to LMWH. Therefore, further larger studies should be able to confirm our hypothesis.
Keywords: Rivaroxaban, Low molecular weight heparin, Total knee arthroplasty, Deep venous thrombosis, Pulmonary embolism, Bleeding outcomes, Novel oral anti-coagulants

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Nowadays major orthopedic surgeries such as total knee arthroplasty (TKA) are becoming more and more common [1]. However, venous thrombo-embolism (VTE) is a life-threatening complication following such surgeries often in the absence of thrombo-prophylaxis [2]. Prophylactic anti-coagulants are often indicated in order to reduce the risk of VTE following TKA [3]. Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) [enoxaparin] has been used following TKA [4]. Recently, novel oral anticoagulants (NAOCs) have widely been made available for thrombo-prophylaxis [5].

Rivaroxaban, a NOAC, has been approved to be used as thrombo-prophylaxis following TKA in the United States [6]. However, most of the studies that systematically assessed the impact of rivaroxaban versus LMWH following TKA showed results with a combination of anti-thrombotic agents or most of the studies showed the clinical outcomes in patients undergoing TKA and hip replacement combined. Studies that systematically assessed the clinical outcomes specifically in patients with TKA were few.

For example, a meta-analysis was carried out to show the effect of rivaroxaban versus enoxaparin for the prevention of VTE after TKA [7]. However, the meta-analysis was specifically based on direct factor Xa inhibitors and included a combination of rivaroxaban and apixaban versus enoxaparin. Other meta-analyses compared rivaroxaban with LMWH for thromboprophylaxis [8], however, they included patients who underwent total hip or knee arthroplasty in combination. Another study was carried out based on prophylaxis using rivaroxaban versus enoxaparin for venous thromboembolism after knee arthroplasty. However, it was a systematic review [9].
In this analysis, we aimed to systematically compare the clinical outcomes observed with rivaroxaban versus LMWH for thrombo-prophylaxis following TKA.

sec.title: Clinical outcomes and definitions
sec.p: The clinical endpoints which were assessed included:
Bleeding outcomes were:

list-item.p: Any bleeding event: was defined as any type of bleeding reported during the study period;

Major bleeding event: included bleeding which was fatal, involving a critical organ, or that required re-operation or clinically overt bleeding outside of the surgical site and which included a decreased hemoglobin level of 2 g or more per deciliter, or requiring the infusion of two or more units of blood;

Non-major bleeding event: was defined as skin and wound hematoma (> 25 cm2 and > 100 cm2 respectively), epistaxis duration greater than 5 min, bleeding at multiple sites or extra-surgical site bleeding and macroscopic hematuria lasting over 24 h;
Minor bleeding event: was defined as bleeding that did not fulfill the criteria for major post-operative bleeding or clinically relevant non major bleeding;
Clinically overt bleeding leading to a decrease in hemoglobin level;
Clinically overt bleeding leading to blood transfusion.

sec.title: Data extraction and quality assessment
sec.p: All the authors who were involved in this research work independently extracted data from the original studies. Following a careful assessment of the original studies, the authors extracted data including the authors’ names, the publication year of each original study, the type of study and the time period when participants were enrolled. In addition, the total number of participants who were assigned to rivaroxaban and LMWH respectively was extracted. The clinical outcomes which were reported, and the number of events associated with each outcome in each separate group (experimental and control groups) were all carefully extracted. Any disagreement which occurred during the data extracted process was carefully discussed among the authors through a discussion panel and a final decision was taken on spot.

The recommendations from the Cochrane Collaboration [10] were used to assess the risk of bias (ROB) observed in randomized trials. However, for the non-randomized studies, the ROB was assessed by the Newcastle Ottawa Scale (NOS) [11].

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analysis was carried out by the Revman software version 5.4. The included studies were added to the software and data associated with the subgroups were input by the authors. Heterogeneity is present in meta-analyses. Heterogeneity was assessed by the Q statistic test and the I2 statistic test. A subgroup with an associated P value less or equal to 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The I2 value was also used to assess heterogeneity whereby the latter was increased with an increasing I2 value. A fix effects statistical model was used if the I2 value was below 50% else a random effects statistical model was used.

An exclusion method was used to show sensitivity analysis. Each study was excluded at a time and a new analysis was carried out each time to observe for any significantly different result from the main analysis. In addition, publication bias was visually observed by assessing symmetry of the funnel plots which were generated from the Revman software.

sec.title: Ethical approval
sec.p: This research was conducted using data from previously published studies. Therefore, an ethical approval was not required for this type of research.

sec.title: Search outcomes
sec.p: The PRISMA guideline was followed [12]. A thorough search from the online databases resulted in a total number of 364 publications. The 364 publications were carefully assessed. The titles and abstracts were carefully read by the authors and an initial elimination was carried out whereby irrelevant publications were directly eliminated. 88 full text articles were assessed for eligibility. Based on the criteria for inclusion and exclusion, further eliminations were carried out as followed:

sec.p: Bias risk assessment of the RCTs was carried out with the recommendations of the Cochrane collaboration and included random sequence generation (selection bias), allocation concealment (selection bias), blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias), blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias), incomplete outcome data (attrition bias), selective reporting (reporting bias) and other bias. A ‘√’ or a ‘x’ was used to show whether the above mentioned components were present or absent and this has been demonstrated in Table 2. Based on the risk of bias assessment shown, most of the RCTs were of good quality.

For the observational studies, bias risk assessment was carried out by the NOS. A 'star system' was used to assess on three broad perspectives: the selection of the study groups (including representative of the exposed cohort, selection of the external control, ascertainment of exposure and outcome of interest not present at the start of the study); the comparability of the groups (main factor and additional factor based on comparability of the cohorts); and the ascertainment of either the exposure or outcome of interest respectively (including assessment of the outcomes, sufficient follow-up time period and adequacy of follow-up). The risk of bias among the observational studies has also been demonstrated in Table 2, a ‘*’ indicated the presence of the respective feature, and a ‘x’ denoted the absence of the corresponding feature.

In 7 studies, data from randomized trials were extracted whereas 2 studies included data from observational studies. The time period for patients’ enrollment varied from year 2004 to year 2016.

sec.title: Main results
sec.p: Our current results showed that DVT (RR: 0.60, 95% CI: 0.51–0.71; P = 0.00001), VTE (RR: 0.56, 95% CI: 0.45–0.70; P = 0.00001), and all-cause mortality (RR: 0.54, 95% CI: 0.33–0.87; P = 0.01) were significantly lower with rivaroxaban compared to LMWH for thrombo-prophylaxis after TKA as shown in Fig. 2. However, the results for PE (RR: 0.54, 95% CI: 0.22–1.31; P = 0.17) and post-operative wound infection (RR: 0.90, 95% CI: 0.73–1.10; P = 0.28) were not significantly different as shown in Fig. 2.

caption.p: Forest plot showing the clinical outcomes between Rivaroxaban and low molecular weight heparin following TKA

sec.p: Our analysis also showed that adverse cardiac events (RR: 1.50, 95% CI: 0.53–4.21; P = 0.44), cardiac death (RR: 1.50, 95% CI: 0.25–9.04; P = 0.66) and MI (RR: 0.33, 95% CI: 0.05–2.11; P = 0.24) were similarly manifested between rivaroxaban and LMWH for thrombo-prophylaxis after TKA as shown in Fig. 3.

caption.p: Forest plot showing the adverse cardiovascular outcomes between Rivaroxaban and low molecular weight heparin following TKA

sec.p: However, any bleeding event (RR: 1.18, 95% CI: 1.07–1.31; P = 0.001), major bleeding (RR: 1.54, 95% CI: 1.12–2.11; P = 0.008), non-major bleeding (RR: 1.15, 95% CI: 1.01–1.30; P = 0.03), minor bleeding (RR: 1.19, 95% CI: 1.06–1.32; P = 0.002) and bleeding leading to re-operation (RR: 1.62, 95% CI: 1.08–2.44; P = 0.02) were significantly higher with rivaroxaban, favoring the use of LMWH as shown in Fig. 4. Nevertheless, clinically overt bleeding leading to a decrease in hemoglobin level (RR: 3.90, 95% CI: 0.93–16.36; P = 0.06), clinically overt bleeding leading to blood transfusion (RR: 2.29, 95% CI: 0.89–5.88; P = 0.09) bleeding through a critical organ (RR: 0.43, 95% CI: 0.06–2.90; P = 0.38) and hemorrhagic wound complication (RR: 1.00, 95% CI: 0.67–1.50; P = 0.99) were not significantly different with rivaroxaban versus LMWH.

sec.p: Sensitivity analysis was carried out. No significantly different result was demonstrated when sensitivity analysis reports were compared with the main results of this analysis. First of all a sensitivity analysis was carried out with randomized trials excluding observational studies (studies Yen2012 and Zou2014 were excluded). The results showed that DVT (RR: 0.62, 95% CI: 0.52–0.73; P = 0.00001), VTE (RR: 0.56, 95% CI: 0.45–0.70; P = 0.00001) and all-cause mortality (RR: 0.54, 95% CI: 0.33–0.87; P = 0.01) were significantly reduced with rivaroxaban. Adverse cardiac events were not significantly different. However, any bleeding event (RR: 1.14, 95% CI: 1.02–1.28; P = 0.02), major bleeding (RR: 1.54, 95% CI: 1.12–2.11; P = 0.008) and minor bleeding (RR: 1.14, 95% CI: 1.01–1.29; P = 0.04) were significantly higher with rivaroxaban. This sensitivity analysis including only RCTs was similar to the main results of our current analysis.

During sensitivity analysis, when study Levitan2014 was excluded and a new analysis was carried out, the result for all-cause mortality (RR: 0.45, 95% CI: 0.10–2.02; P = 0.30) was not significantly different showing that the result for all cause mortality was influenced by study Levitan2014. In addition, when study Levitan2014 was excluded and a new analysis was carried out, the result for major bleeding (RR: 1.46, 95% CI: 0.76–2.77; P = 0.25) was not significantly different which was different from our main result.
Exclusion of the remaining studies by turn did not affect the main results of this analysis.

The Cochrane Handbook suggests at least 10 studies for Egger’s test interpretation. With fewer than 10 studies included in this meta-analysis, the Egger’s test was not recommended based on guidelines, due to lack of statistical power making results unreliable and inconclusive. Hence, publication bias was visually assessed through two funnel plots (Figs. 5 and 6), and based on this visual assessment, there was low evidence of bias across studies that were involved to assess this comparison of rivaroxaban versus LMWH following TKA.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Our analysis showed a significantly lower number of thrombotic events with rivaroxaban but an increased risk of bleeding outcomes when compared to LMWH for thrombo-prophylaxis following TKA.

The mechanisms of action of rivaroxaban [22] and enoxaparin are different. Rivaroxaban is a direct competitive reversible antagonist of activated factor Xa, which is the active component of the prothombinase complex that is responsible for the conversion of prothombin to thrombin. In other words, rivaroxaban works by inhibiting Factor Xa, which is an important factor of the blood clotting cascade, which then prevents the formation of thrombin and therefore prevent clot formation. It has an onset of action which begins 30 min after the drug has been taken and it has a duration of action of 24 h. On the other hand, enoxaparin works differently and is an indirect anticoagulant that binds and activates anti-thrombin III to form a complex that preferentially inactivates factor Xa, preventing thrombosis [23].

A recent meta-analysis compared rivaroxaban versus enoxaparin for the prevention of VTE and wound complications after TKA [24]. Six studies with a total number of 6627 participants were included. Similar to our current meta-analysis, VTE and DVT were significantly reduced with rivaroxaban. However, unlike our current analysis, major bleeding was not significantly increased with rivaroxaban.

A few meta-analyses have been published on this particular subject, however, they were not based uniquely on patients undergoing TKA. For example, a systematic review and meta-analysis based on the safety and efficacy of NOACs versus LMWH for thrombo-prophylaxis after TKA or total hip replacement was published and the results indeed showed NOACs to significantly reduce the risk of DVT and adverse events [25]. Subgroup analyses also showed respective NOACs including rivaroxaban, apixaban and edoxaban to significantly reduce the risk of DVT when compared to LMWH. Apixaban showed to have a significantly lower risk of bleeding in comparison to LMWH following TKA. However, our current analysis showed significantly higher bleeding risks with rivaroxaban.

A previous meta-analysis of randomized trial comparing rivaroxaban versus enoxaparin for thrombo-prophylaxis after total hip or TKA involving 15,586 participants showed rivaroxaban to be more effective than enoxaparin without affecting bleeding outcomes [26]. However, in this current meta-analysis, bleeding outcomes including major and minor bleedings were significantly higher with rivaroxaban. It should also be noted that the previous analysis consisted of participants who underwent TKA as well as those who underwent surgery for total hip replacement, whereas our current analysis consisted only of patients who underwent TKA.

Our current analysis showed lower number of thrombotic events including VTE and DVT but an increased risk of bleeding outcomes with rivaroxaban compared to LMWH for thrombo-prophylaxis following TKA. Similarly, a retrospective cohort study consisting of participants from 121 hospitals based in Canada showed similar efficacy outcomes [27]. The authors even concluded that rivaroxaban compared to LMWH after hospital discharge was associated with a significantly decreased risk of symptomatic VTE without affecting the bleeding risk. However, in our current analysis, only after excluding study Levitan2014 that major bleeding was not significantly higher with rivaroxaban.

In another cohort study from the Chelsea and Westminster Hospital in the United Kingdom [28], 479 participants who received thrombo-prophylaxis following knee of hip surgery were investigated and the authors showed that rivaroxaban was effective and safe to use for thrombo-prophylaxis after similar kind of surgeries. However, in our current analysis, the safety profile of rivaroxaban was doubtful.

Our analysis has demonstrated significantly lower thrombotic outcomes with rivaroxaban when compared to LMWH for thrombo-prophylaxis after TKA. However, major and minor bleeding events were significantly higher with rivaroxaban. In contrast, our sensitivity reports showed the results for major bleeding to have been affected by study Levitan2014, and excluding this study showed similar major bleeding between rivaroxaban and LMWH for TKA, with significantly higher minor bleeding.

A newly published analysis [29] based on the impact of direct factor Xa inhibitors versus LMWH or vitamin K antagonists for the prevention of VTE in elective or primary hip or knee replacement or hip fracture repair, which included 53 randomized trials showed direct factor Xa inhibitors like rivaroxaban could have slightly reduced the risk of symptomatic VTE compared to LMWH but the evidence is not certain. In addition, rivaroxaban resulted in a slightly increased risk of major bleeding compared to LMWH similar to our analysis. However, the other direct factor Xa inhibitors were not associated with any major bleeding, but the evidence was not certain.

In patients with higher bleeding risks, for example elderly patients, if rivaroxaban is associated with high bleeding events following TKA, LMWH might be considered instead of rivaroxaban, and mechanical prophylaxis such as compression stocking could help. The treatment would be based on specific clinical situations or on a case to case basis to balance thrombotic risk with bleeding risk. Bleeding risk assessment tools could also be considered as another option.

Similar to rivaroxaban, other NOACs are also being used for thrombo-prophylaxis following TKA. For example, in the RE-MODEL trial, the authors demonstrated the use of dabigatran versus enoxaparin for the prevention of VTE after TKA [30]. In their study, the authors showed that dabigatran, in two different doses were equally tolerable in comparison with enoxaparin without any significant increase in thrombotic outcomes or major bleeding events following TKA. Another retrospective study including 200 participants who underwent TKA showed the efficacy of apixaban in comparison to enoxaparin, and the results demonstrated no significant difference between these two anticoagulants regarding minor and major wound complications as well as the occurrence of thrombotic events, indicating apixaban as an alternative to enoxaparin for the prevention of thrombo-embolism following TKA [31].

NOACs are gradually replacing older anticoagulants. The implication of this analysis was to show the efficacy and safety outcomes of rivaroxaban versus LMWH (enoxaparin) for thrombo-prophylaxis following TKA. This might help orthopaedic surgeons in view of decision taking when preparing a patient for TKA or post-operatively to reduce the chances of thrombotic events as well as reducing bleeding risks.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: This analysis also has limitations. First of all, we have included both randomized trials and observational studies together and analyzed. This could have a minor effect on the final outcomes. However, most of the studies were randomized trials and therefore the main outcomes would not be heavily affected. Another limitation could be the fact that the time periods during which all those events happened were not taken into consideration. In a few studies the number of event was reported during the 2 days post-operative periods whereas in other studies, this time varied. In addition, the dosage of rivaroxaban varied in a few studies. Different dosages could affect the main results of this analysis. Also, several studies did not clearly mention about the dosage of drugs being used, or the comparison was not made between different dosages of drugs. Hence, we could not carry out a separate analysis based on dosage of rivaroxaban or enoxaparin. Hence, this could be another limitation of this study. Study Levitan2014 consisted of 20,000 participants and this study could partially have affected the main results of this analysis. However, sensitivity analysis has demonstrated that only the results for all-cause mortality and major bleeding were influenced by study Levitan2014 by showing significantly different results when the study was excluded. This could be another limitation of this analysis. At last, sensitivity analyses ignore time-to-event differences in outcomes, potentially confounding results and this could be another limitation.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Our analysis showed that rivaroxaban when used as thrombo-prophylaxis following TKA, significantly reduced thrombotic outcomes when compared to LMWH. However, the risks of bleeding events including major and minor bleeding events were significantly increased in comparison to LMWH. Therefore, further larger studies should be able to confirm our hypothesis.
